title: Nominative and accusative: subject and object

objectives.can: Tell a nominative from an accusative and say which is the subject and which the object of a clause.

explanation.summary: In Greek the ending of a noun, not its place in the sentence, shows who is doing something and what it is being done to. The nominative usually marks the subject; the accusative usually marks the direct object.

sections.heading: The ending does the work
body: English tells subject from object by word order: 'the father loves the son' is not 'the son loves the father'. Greek tells them by case. A noun in the nominative is, in the ordinary clause, the subject. A noun in the accusative is, in the ordinary clause, the direct object: the person or thing the action reaches.

This is why you can usually trust the article and the ending, and need not trust the position. The verb often comes first or last, and the object often comes before the subject, whenever the author wants to stress something.

sections.heading: Signals to look for
body: The article is the quickest guide, because its nominative and accusative forms differ in the masculine and feminine: ὁ and τὸν, ἡ and τὴν, οἱ and τοὺς, αἱ and τὰς. The noun's own ending usually agrees, but the pairs are not alike in every declension. Learn the article first and let it confirm the noun.

head: Where the forms differ
Nominative
Accusative
rows: Masculine of the common -ος type, singular
Feminine of the common -η type, singular
Feminine of the common -α type, singular
varies: a stem plus -ς, or the bare stem

sections.heading: The neuter: nominative and accusative alike
body: In every neuter noun, and in the neuter article, the nominative and accusative are identical, singular and plural. So τὸ πνεῦμα may be the subject of one clause and the object of another. Only the rest of the sentence decides. The verse in the examples below shows both.

sections.heading: The predicate nominative
body: With εἰμί ('I am') and a few verbs of becoming, the word that says what the subject is stands in the same case as the subject: the nominative. Both nouns are nominative, so neither is an object. When both have the article, either could in principle be the subject; usually the one with the article is the subject and the other says what it is. Look at the examples for how this works in John and in the First Letter of John.

sections.heading: Other uses of the accusative
body: The accusative is not only the case of the direct object. It is also the case that follows many prepositions (πρὸς τὸν θεόν, εἰς τὸν κόσμον), and it can express how long or how far. A noun after a preposition is not a direct object, even though it is accusative. Which case a preposition takes is part of learning the preposition; for now, notice that the accusative has more work than 'object'.

misunderstandings: Do not read the first noun as the subject. Greek word order is free: in the examples, the subject sometimes follows the verb or follows the predicate.
A neuter noun looks the same as subject and as object. Do not call it a nominative or an accusative from its form alone: look at the verb and the other words.
A noun in the accusative after a preposition is not the object of the verb. The preposition governs it.
Two nominatives with εἰμί are not subject and object. The second names what the first is.

deeper.heading: Why the accusative is so wide
body: Grammarians have long noted that the accusative is the least specific of the cases: it says that a noun is connected with the action, and the verb or preposition shows how. That is why one case can serve for an object, a goal after εἰς, and a stretch of time. Treat 'direct object' as the common case and not the only one.

examples.analysis: ὁ πατήρ is nominative singular masculine: the subject of ἀγαπᾷ, 'loves'. τὸν υἱόν is accusative singular masculine: the object, the one who is loved. The article and the noun agree, and the article ὁ against τὸν already shows which is which.

examples.analysis: The subject ὁ θεός is nominative; the objects are both accusative: τὸν κόσμον after ἠγάπησεν ('loved the world') and τὸν υἱόν after ἔδωκεν ('gave the Son'). The subject stands after its verb, the objects before theirs. The case endings, not the order, tell the roles.
